steps.formula: ΣWX / ΣW = Σ CO₂ / Σ population

time_series.decomposition_note: Annual data: no seasonal component exists; only the trend (centred MA) is estimated.

concepts.objective: Structure the project the way the course defines the data science process.
concepts.interpretation: The project follows the course framework: questions first, then data understanding and preparation, then modelling and evaluation, then a dashboard that reports the knowledge gained.
concepts.validation: Each stage has its own module and tests.

concepts.interpretation: 50,411 observations is the 'volume' motivation from Module 1; with 79 attributes, picking relevant variables (feature selection) matters.
concepts.validation: Shape asserted in tests/test_data.py::test_shape_and_keys; file hash checked against MANIFEST.json.

concepts.interpretation: (country, year) is a valid unique key, so no rows need dropping for duplication.
concepts.validation: tests/test_data.py::test_shape_and_keys

concepts.interpretation: Regions, income groups and duplicate '(GCP)' regions sit in the same table as countries. Summing them together would double-count, so every analysis filters entity_type = country.
concepts.validation: World total reconciles with Σ countries + international aviation & shipping to within 0.5% (tests/test_data.py::test_world_equals_countries_plus_international).

concepts.interpretation: A blank means 'not reported', never zero emissions. Each analysis drops missing values only for the columns it uses (listwise per analysis), and reports its own n.
concepts.validation: tests/test_data.py::test_clean_keeps_every_row_and_value checks no value was imputed.

concepts.interpretation: No impossible values. Negative land-use or growth values are real (carbon sinks, falling emissions) and are kept. Early zeros are years before a country's record starts. Extreme values (e.g. Qatar) are genuine and are flagged, not deleted.
concepts.validation: Flags stored as columns (flag_negative_nonneg_col, flag_zero_co2, fuel_sum_gap).

output.Used for: LOF distances; regression on log scale

concepts.interpretation: Per-person CO₂ and GDP are strongly right-skewed with a heavy upper tail. Logging removes the heavy tail (β₂ close to the normal value 3, and the empirical rule holds), though a mild left skew remains from the very lowest emitters. Min–max scaling stops one unit from dominating a distance.
concepts.validation: Range of scaled column is exactly [0, 1].

concepts.variables: log CO₂pc ~ log GDPpc + log energy pc (2022)

output.Hold-out (2/3 train): train n=109, test n=55, test R² = 0.938

concepts.interpretation: Cross-validated R² is close to the in-sample R², so the regression is not overfitting. Every country is used for validation exactly once.
concepts.validation: tests/test_cross_checks.py::test_kfold_uses_every_record_once; fixed seed 42.

concepts.formula: \text{resample } n \text{ values with replacement, } B = 5000 \text{ times}
concepts.interpretation: The median has no simple standard-error formula; bootstrapping gives an interval for it straight from the data.
concepts.validation: Same seed gives the same interval (tests/test_cross_checks.py::test_bootstrap_reproducible).

concepts.interpretation: Richer countries emit more per person, but GDP does not 'cause' CO₂ by itself: energy use and energy mix sit in between (see the multiple regression). All findings are worded as associations.
concepts.validation: Multiple regression shows GDP loses significance once energy is controlled.

concepts.concept: Types of data / levels of measurement
concepts.variables: country, continent, year, co2, co2_per_capita, growth %
concepts.interpretation: Ratio variables support every statistic (means, ratios, CV). Interval ones (year) do not have a true zero, so 'twice as many years' is meaningless.
concepts.validation: Mapping shown on the Dataset Explorer page.

concepts.interpretation: Most countries emit little per person, with a long tail of high emitters: a positively skewed distribution.
concepts.validation: Σf equals n (tests/test_cross_checks.py::test_grouped_formulas_consistent).

concepts.interpretation: The two-way table is also the input of the two-way ANOVA (Module 3).
concepts.validation: Built from country rows only, so no aggregate is double-counted.

concepts.formula: \bar X = \frac{\Sigma X}{N};\quad \bar X = A + \frac{\Sigma f d'}{N}\times i
concepts.interpretation: The grouped mean differs from the exact mean because it assumes values sit at class mid-points. The lower quantiles suffer most, because nearly half the countries fall in the first class. With raw data available, the individual-series value is the one to report.
concepts.validation: Short-cut = direct and step-deviation = direct (tests/test_cross_checks.py).

concepts.formula: \bar X_w = \frac{\Sigma W X}{\Sigma W};\quad \bar X_{12} = \frac{N_1\bar X_1 + N_2 \bar X_2}{N_1+N_2}
concepts.interpretation: The simple mean treats Tuvalu and India equally; the weighted mean gives the average for a person. The weighted value is a little below the World figure because international aviation and shipping belong to no country.
concepts.validation: Combined mean of continent groups reproduces the overall mean exactly.

concepts.interpretation: Mode < Median < Mean: the order the course gives for a positively skewed distribution. Continuous values never repeat exactly, so the mode comes from the grouped formula.
concepts.validation: Grouped median lies within one class width of the exact median.

concepts.interpretation: A quarter of countries emit under 0.99 t per person; the top 10% emit over 11.18 t.
concepts.validation: Equals numpy's 'weibull' quantile method, which is the (N+1) rule (tests/test_cross_checks.py).

concepts.interpretation: The range is driven by a single country (Qatar); the IQR describes the middle half and is not affected by extremes.
concepts.validation: Hand formulas; quartiles cross-checked.

concepts.interpretation: A CV above 100% means the spread is larger than the average itself: countries are extremely unequal emitters.
concepts.validation: Matches numpy.std (ddof 0 and 1); assumed-mean method equals actual-mean method.

concepts.interpretation: All three are positive (right skew). Bowley is much smaller because it only looks at the middle 50% and ignores the long tail of extreme emitters.
concepts.validation: Signs agree with Mean > Median.

output.Shape: Leptokurtic (more peaked, heavier tails than normal)

concepts.interpretation: β₂ far above 3: a sharp peak of low emitters plus heavy tails. (The course formula sheet's shape descriptions are swapped; the standard meaning is used here.)
concepts.validation: Equals scipy.stats.kurtosis(fisher=False, bias=True).

output.Examples: Qatar, Kuwait, Brunei, Bahrain, Trinidad and Tobago

concepts.interpretation: The flagged countries are genuine (mostly oil- and gas-exporting states, plus large energy-intensive economies such as Australia and the US), not data errors, so they are kept and discussed.
concepts.validation: Count reproduced on the Descriptive Statistics page for any year.

concepts.variables: continent, year, change since 2005, largest fuel source, co2_per_capita (2024)
concepts.formula: \text{group facts into classes sharing one characteristic}

output.Geographical: Asia 60.6% of world CO₂ from 50 countries
output.Chronological: world mean annual CO₂ by decade, 1950s → 2020–2024
output.Quantitative: 5 magnitude classes of CO₂ per person

concepts.interpretation: Each type answers a different question: where (continent), when (decade), what kind (attribute) and how much (magnitude).
concepts.validation: Class counts sum to the number of countries; continent totals use countries only.

concepts.concept: Tabulation: simple, two-way and higher-order tables
concepts.interpretation: In the two-way table, 38 of Africa's 55 countries emit under 1 t per person; most European countries sit between 3 and 10 t.
concepts.validation: Row and column totals reproduce the one-way table (pandas crosstab with margins).

concepts.concept: Discrete series: mean, median, mode, quartiles, σ
concepts.variables: years with falling CO₂, 2006–2024 per country (n = 214)
concepts.formula: \bar X = \frac{\Sigma fX}{N};\ \text{Median} = X \text{ at } cf \ge \tfrac{N+1}{2};\ \sigma = \sqrt{\tfrac{\Sigma fd^2}{N} - \left(\tfrac{\Sigma fd}{N}\right)^2}
concepts.interpretation: A typical country saw its emissions fall in about 7 of the 19 years; mean, median and mode are close, so this count is roughly symmetric, unlike per-person emissions.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the course examples (marks mean 41, median income ₹16,800, P20 = Q1 = D3 = 20, Q3 = 40).

concepts.concept: Inclusive → exclusive classes; class limits from mid-values
concepts.formula: L' = L - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{gap},\ U' = U + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{gap};\ \ L = m - \tfrac{i}{2},\ U = m + \tfrac{i}{2}
concepts.interpretation: Whole-number classes leave gaps (3 to 4); converting to exclusive classes makes the series continuous so the interpolation formulas apply.
concepts.validation: Tested on simple inclusive classes and the slide's mid-value example (115 → 110–120).

concepts.formula: \text{Median} = \text{x where the two ogives cross} = L + \frac{N/2 - cf}{f}\times i
concepts.interpretation: The graphical and formula medians agree exactly, because the ogive interpolates linearly inside the median class just as the formula does.
concepts.validation: Tested on the course 'median from cumulative data' example. The slide uses i = 10 for classes 5 wide and prints 14.29; the correct median is 12.15.

concepts.variables: CO₂ per person (t), 2024, n = 214 countries; last class '15 t and above'
concepts.formula: \text{assume open class width} = \text{neighbour's width, then } \bar X = \frac{\Sigma fm}{N}
concepts.interpretation: The open-class mean depends on an assumption about the missing limit; the median does not. With an open top class in skewed data, report the median, as the course advises.
concepts.validation: Tested on the course example ('Below 10' … 'Above 50').

concepts.concept: Correcting incorrect items in a mean
concepts.interpretation: If regional totals are averaged in with countries by mistake, the course correction formula recovers the countries-only mean exactly: a concrete reason the cleaning step matters.
concepts.validation: Reproduces Illustrations 6 and 7 (39.7 and 40.18).

concepts.concept: Moments (about origin and mean), β₁, β₂ & empirical mode
concepts.interpretation: μ₃ > 0 confirms right skew and μ₄ the heavy tail. The empirical mode relation only holds for moderate skew; here it is far from the grouped mode, another sign of extreme skewness.
concepts.validation: Central moments computed directly and from raw moments agree; γ₁ and β₂ match SciPy.

concepts.interpretation: Distance from the multivariate centre (in SD units) is a first, simple outlier screen.
concepts.validation: Means computed directly.

concepts.formula: r = \frac{\Sigma xy}{\sqrt{\Sigma x^2\,\Sigma y^2}} = \frac{N\Sigma XY - \Sigma X\Sigma Y}{\sqrt{N\Sigma X^2-(\Sigma X)^2}\sqrt{N\Sigma Y^2-(\Sigma Y)^2}}
concepts.interpretation: A strong positive relationship that is clearer on the log scale, because both variables are skewed. r² = share of variation in one explained by the other.
concepts.validation: Actual-mean, direct and assumed-mean methods agree to 1e-12; equal to numpy.corrcoef.

concepts.concept: Types of correlation: positive, negative, none, non-linear
concepts.variables: cross-section 2022 (n = 164), UK 1990–2024, population vs CO₂ pc 2024
concepts.interpretation: Richer countries emit more per person but have cleaner energy per kWh. Population says nothing about per-person emissions. Raw GDP vs CO₂ is curved, so r understates the link until both are logged.
concepts.validation: Each r computed with the course method; signs match the scatter diagrams.

concepts.variables: log₁₀ CO₂ pc (y), log₁₀ GDP pc (x₁), log₁₀ energy pc (x₂), 2022
concepts.interpretation: Holding energy constant removes almost all of GDP's link with emissions, the correlation-side view of the regression's multicollinearity result. Multiple R² equals the regression R².
concepts.validation: Partial r equals the correlation of residuals (statsmodels); multiple R equals √R² of OLS.

concepts.concept: Diagrams & graphs: bars (simple, multiple, sub-divided, percentage, deviation, broken), rectangle, square, circle, pie, pictogram, cartogram, line (incl. false baseline), histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, box plot, distribution chart, scatter, scatter matrix, bubble

output.Charts in dashboard: all of these, with units and tooltips
output.Rectangle diagram: width = population, height = CO₂ per person, area = total CO₂

concepts.interpretation: Line for trends, bars for comparisons, two-dimensional shapes when area should carry the value, histogram/box/ogive for distributions, scatter/bubble/scatter matrix for relationships.
concepts.validation: Every chart is drawn from computed data, never hard-coded.

concepts.variables: CO₂ per person (t), 2024, n = 214 countries and its log₁₀
concepts.interpretation: Raw per-person emissions are far from normal; their logarithm is close to normal (log-normal distribution). This is why tests and regression use the log scale.
concepts.validation: Normal percentages from scipy.stats.norm.

concepts.variables: Yearly count of countries (≥1 Mt) whose CO₂ fell by >10%, 1991–2024
concepts.interpretation: Variance is about five times the mean, so these counts are NOT Poisson: drops cluster in crisis years (2020: 42 countries, 2009: 27, 1991–94 post-Soviet collapse: 17–23 a year) instead of happening independently at a constant rate.
concepts.validation: Index-of-dispersion χ² test, n − 1 d.f.

concepts.variables: CO₂ per person (t), 2024, n = 214 countries; 10,000 samples of n = 30
concepts.formula: \bar X \sim N\!\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right) \text{ for large } n
concepts.interpretation: Even from this strongly skewed population, sample means are nearly normal and their spread matches σ/√n: the CLT on real data.
concepts.validation: Seeded simulation (seed 42).

concepts.interpretation: Read as: if 2024 countries were a sample from the process that generates national emissions, the mean per-person value lies in this range with 95% confidence. The 214 countries are a near-complete set, so this is a model-based interpretation.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the course example (45 ± 2.77) in tests.

concepts.interpretation: The average country is not significantly different from the average person at 5%. Large spread between countries makes the test weak.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the oceanographer example (Z = 2.067) in tests.

concepts.interpretation: Average per-person emissions fell significantly since 2005, yet more countries rose than fell: large falls in high emitters (Europe, North America) outweigh many small rises.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the soldiers example (|t| = 2.16); p matches scipy.ttest_rel.

concepts.variables: log₁₀ CO₂ per person, Europe (n=44) vs Asia (n=50), 2024
concepts.interpretation: Typical (geometric-mean) values: Europe 5.03 t vs Asia 3.54 t. The difference is not significant at 5%, and the large variance ratio means the pooled-variance assumption is questionable, so Welch's version is also reported.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the diet example; p matches scipy.ttest_ind.

concepts.variables: CO₂ per person (t), 2024, n = 214 countries; 10,000 simulated samples of n = 40
concepts.formula: \alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 | H_0 \text{ true}),\ \beta = P(\text{accept } H_0 | H_0 \text{ false})
concepts.interpretation: With skewed data and n = 40 the z-test rejects a true H₀ more often than 5%: the normal approximation is not yet accurate. β shows how often a real 1.5 t difference would be missed.
concepts.validation: Type I rate converges toward α as n grows (try it on the Statistical Analysis page).

concepts.variables: log₁₀ CO₂ per person by continent (2024, k = 6, n = 214)
concepts.interpretation: Continent explains a large share (η²) of the variation in log emissions per person. Group sizes differ, so the grand mean is weighted by n (the slides' 'mean of means' only works for equal groups).
concepts.validation: Reproduces the wheat example (F = 1.5); matches scipy.f_oneway; SS_T = SS_B + SS_W.

concepts.variables: continental CO₂ per person: continent (rows) × year (columns)
concepts.interpretation: Differences between continents are significant; differences between years are not, because continents moved in opposite directions (Asia up, Europe and North America down), which ends up in the residual.
concepts.validation: Matches statsmodels anova_lm (tests).

concepts.variables: y = log₁₀ CO₂ pc, x = log₁₀ GDP pc (2022, n = 164)
concepts.formula: a = \frac{n\Sigma xy - \Sigma x\Sigma y}{n\Sigma x^2 - (\Sigma x)^2},\ \ b = \frac{\Sigma y - a\Sigma x}{n}
concepts.interpretation: On log scales the slope is an elasticity: a 1% higher GDP per person goes with about 1.04% higher CO₂ per person, on average across countries (association, not causation).
concepts.validation: Reproduces the expenditure example (a = 8.4, b = 3.2); matches statsmodels OLS.

concepts.concept: Error measures: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, R²
concepts.formula: MAE=\tfrac1n\Sigma|y-\hat y|,\ RMSE=\sqrt{\tfrac1n\Sigma(y-\hat y)^2},\ MAPE=\tfrac{100}{n}\Sigma\left|\tfrac{y-\hat y}{y}\right|,\ R^2 = 1-\tfrac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}
concepts.interpretation: MAPE is computed after converting predictions back to tonnes, because on the log scale values near 0 make MAPE meaningless (a limitation the slides mention).
concepts.validation: Hand formulas; R² matches statsmodels.

concepts.concept: Multiple linear regression & partial regression coefficients
concepts.variables: y = log₁₀ CO₂ pc; X₁ = log₁₀ GDP pc; X₂ = log₁₀ energy pc (2022, n = 164)
concepts.formula: b_1 = \frac{\Sigma x_2^2\Sigma x_1y - \Sigma x_1x_2\Sigma x_2y}{\Sigma x_1^2\Sigma x_2^2 - (\Sigma x_1x_2)^2},\ b_0 = \bar Y - b_1\bar X_1 - b_2\bar X_2
concepts.interpretation: Holding energy use constant, GDP adds almost nothing; holding GDP constant, 1% more energy per person goes with about 1% more CO₂ per person. GDP and energy are highly correlated (multicollinearity), so the GDP coefficient is unstable.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the course example (b1 = 3.1479, b2 = −1.6561, R² = 0.9626); matches statsmodels.

concepts.interpretation: The model as a whole is highly significant (F-test first, as the slides require); individually only energy per person is significant at 5%.
concepts.validation: SE and t match statsmodels (tests/test_cross_checks.py).

concepts.variables: min–max scaled log₁₀ GDP pc & log₁₀ CO₂ pc (2022, n = 164), k = 10

output.Top 5 by LOF: Qatar (2.37), North Korea (1.86), Norway (1.67), Switzerland (1.59), Venezuela (1.59)

concepts.interpretation: LOF finds countries that are unusual for their neighbourhood: very high emitters for their income (Qatar), and also low emitters for their income (Switzerland, Sweden, North Korea's low GDP with relatively high CO₂). The IQR rule only sees one variable and only high values.
concepts.validation: Reproduces the 4-point slide example (LOF(d) = 2.0); matches sklearn LocalOutlierFactor(metric='manhattan').

concepts.formula: Y = T + S + R \ \text{or}\ Y = T\times S\times R;\ T = \text{centred MA}

output.Seasonal component: not applicable (annual data, no within-year seasons)

concepts.interpretation: Seasonality needs sub-annual data. On annual CO₂ only the trend and irregular parts exist; the years in which world emissions fell match known shocks: 1974–75 and 1980–82 (oil crises), 1992 (post-Soviet collapse), 2009 (financial crisis) and 2020 (COVID, −5.2%).
concepts.validation: Additive and multiplicative decomposition reproduce the slide example exactly (tests).

concepts.concept: Average, moving-average & naïve forecasts; least-squares trend
concepts.formula: F_t=\tfrac{1}{t-1}\Sigma_{i<t} y_i;\ \ F_t=\tfrac1k\Sigma_{i=t-k}^{t-1}y_i;\ \ \hat y = a\,t + b
concepts.interpretation: Best on the hold-out by MASE: Naïve (last value). The 2000–2019 linear trend overshoots because emissions growth slowed after 2013 and dropped in 2020. The average method is useless for a trending series, exactly as the slides warn.
concepts.validation: Reproduces slide metrics (MAE 2.32, MASE 1.16 / 2.67, 1.14).

concepts.concept: Forecast evaluation: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE
concepts.interpretation: MASE above 1 for every method shows that, over 2020–2024, simply carrying forward last year's value is hard to beat for annual emissions.
concepts.validation: Hand formulas; slide examples reproduced.
